title: Derivation of the Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation for Small Amplitude Deep Water Waves from a Non-Local Formulation
text:
We start by defining the domain
\[
D=\{-\infty<x<\infty,\quad -h<y<\eta(x, t),\quad t>0\}
\]
The classical gravity water wave problem satisfies
\[
\Delta\phi=0\quad\text{in }D,
\tag{1}\] \[
\phi_y=0\quad\text{on }y=-h,
\tag{2}\] \[
\eta_t+\phi_x\eta_x=\phi_y\quad\text{on }y=\eta,
\tag{3}\] \[
\phi_t+\frac{1}{2}|\nabla\phi|^2+g\eta=\frac{\sigma\eta_{xx}}{\rho(1+\eta_x^2)^\frac{3}{2}}\quad\text{on }y=\eta.
\tag{4}\]

title: Derivation of the Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation for Small Amplitude Deep Water Waves from a Non-Local Formulation

We start by defining the domain
\[
D=\{-\infty<x<\infty,\quad -h<y<\eta(x, t),\quad t>0\}
\]
The classical gravity water wave problem satisfies
\[
\Delta\phi=0\quad\text{in }D,
\tag{1}\] \[
\phi_y=0\quad\text{on }y=-h,
\tag{2}\] \[
\eta_t+\phi_x\eta_x=\phi_y\quad\text{on }y=\eta,
\tag{3}\] \[
\phi_t+\frac{1}{2}|\nabla\phi|^2+g\eta=\frac{\sigma\eta_{xx}}{\rho(1+\eta_x^2)^\frac{3}{2}}\quad\text{on }y=\eta.
\tag{4}\]

title: Derivation of the Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation for Small Amplitude Deep Water Waves from a Non-Local Formulation
text:
Deriving the Dynamic Boundary Condition
We aim to reformulate these equations purely in terms of functions on the free boundary. These functions are \(\eta(x, t)\) and \(q(x, t):=\phi(x_1, \eta(x, t), t)\).
Since Equation 3 is satisfied on the free surface, and
\[
\phi_x+\phi_y\eta_x=q_x,
\]
we have
\[
\eta_t+[q_x-\phi_y\eta_x]\eta_x=\phi_y
\] \[
\implies\phi_y=\frac{\eta_x q_x+\eta_t}{1+\eta_x^2},\quad\phi_x=\frac{q_x-\eta_x\eta_t}{1+\eta_x^2}.
\]
This implies that
\[
|\nabla\phi|^2=\phi_x^2+\phi_y^2
\] \[
=\frac{[q_x^2-2\eta_x\eta_t q_x+\eta_x^2\eta_t^2]+[\eta_x^2 q_x^2+2\eta_x\eta_t q_x+\eta_t^2]}{(1+\eta_x^2)^2}
\] \[
=\frac{[q_x^2+\eta_t^2]+\eta_x^2[q_x^2+\eta_t^2]}{(1+\eta_x^2)^2}
\] \[
=\frac{q_x^2+\eta_t^2}{1+\eta_x^2}
\]
Substituting \(|\nabla\phi|^2\) and \(\phi_t=q_t-\phi_y\eta_t\) into Equation 4, we have
\[
[q_t-\left[\frac{\eta_x q_x+\eta_t}{1+\eta_x^2}\right]\eta_t]+\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{q_x^2+\eta_t^2}{1+\eta_x^2}\right]+g\eta=\frac{\sigma\eta_{xx}}{\rho(1+\eta_x^2)^\frac{3}{2}}
\] \[
\implies q_t+g\eta-\frac{\sigma\eta_{xx}}{\rho(1+\eta_x^2)^\frac{3}{2}}+\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{q_x^2+\eta_t^2}{1+\eta_x^2}-\frac{2\eta_x\eta_t q_x+2\eta_t^2}{1+\eta_x^2}\right)=0
\] \[
\implies q_t+g\eta-\frac{\sigma\eta_{xx}}{\rho(1+\eta_x^2)^\frac{3}{2}}+\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{(1+\eta_x^2)q_x^2}{1+\eta_x^2}-\frac{\eta_x^2q_x^2+2\eta_x\eta_t q_x+\eta_t^2}{1+\eta_x^2}\right)=0
\] \[
\implies q_t+g\eta-\frac{\sigma\eta_{xx}}{\rho(1+\eta_x^2)^\frac{3}{2}}+\frac{1}{2}q_x^2-\frac{(\eta_t+\eta_x q_x)^2}{1+\eta_x^2}=0
\] This is the dynamic boundary condition - Bernoulli’s equation.

title: Derivation of the Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation for Small Amplitude Deep Water Waves from a Non-Local Formulation
text:
Deriving the Global Relation
Suppose that \(\phi(x,y)\) and \(\psi(x,y)\) are harmonic functions in \(D\) - i.e. they satisfy Equation 1. Then we have the identity
\[
\phi_y(\psi_{xx}+\psi_{yy})+\psi_y(\phi_{xx}+\phi_{yy})=0.
\]
Which can be rewritten as
\[
(\phi_y\psi_x+\phi_x\psi_y)_x+(\phi_y\psi_y-\phi_x\psi_x)_y=0.
\]
Now let \(\psi(x,y)=e^{ikx+ky}\). Since \(\psi\) is harmonic, we can write
\[
[\psi(ik\phi_y+k\phi_x)]_x+[\psi(k\phi_x-ik\phi_x)]_y=0
\]
In other words, the vector field \(\vec{F}(x,y)=\psi(ik\phi_y+k\phi_x)\hat{i}+\psi(k\phi_x-ik\phi_x)\hat{j}\) is non-divergent - i.e. \(\nabla\cdot F=0\). Since \(F\) is a continuously differentiable vector field,
\[
\int_D[\nabla\cdot F]dV=\int_{\partial D}[F\cdot\hat{n}]dS
\]
by the divergence theorem. Thus,
\[
\int_{\partial D}[e^{ikx+ky}[(ik\phi_y+k\phi_x)\hat{i}+(k\phi_y-ik\phi_x)\hat{j}]\cdot\hat{n}]dS=0
\]
Here, we make the assumption that \(\eta\) and \(|\nabla\phi|\) vanish as \(|x|\to\infty\) (the physical interpretation of this assumption is that waters are calm very far away from the waves we are observing). Thus we have
\[
\lim_{|x|\to\infty}\left(\int_{\partial D}[F\cdot\hat{n}]dS\right)=\int_{-\infty}^\infty([F\cdot\hat{n}]_{y=-h}+[F\cdot\hat{n}]_{y=\eta})dx=0
\]

title: Subcritical Hopf Bifurcations, and Other Horrors Lurking in the Night
text:
Limit Cycles
Definition
A limit cycle is an isolated closed trajectory in phase space.
Brief Description
Recall that a closed trajectory in the phase space of a dynamical system represents a periodic solution. So a limit cycle describes a periodic solution that is isolated from all other periodic solutions - i.e. there are no other closed trajectories in a small neighbourhood around a limit cycle.
Limit cycles only exist in nonlinear systems. If \(\pmb{x}(t)\) is a periodic solution to a linear system \(\dot{\pmb{x}}=A\pmb{x}\), then \(c\pmb{x}(t)\) is also a solution for any constant \(c\in\mathbb{R}\). So for any linear system, either no closed trajectories exist, or an infinite family of closed trajectories exist.
A limit cycle is said to be stable if all neighbouring trajectories converge to the limit cycle, and unstable if all neighbouring trajectories diverge from the limit cycle. Half-stable limit cycles exist as well, but are difficult to generalize to phase spaces of dimension \(3\) or higher. In the phase plane, a half-stable limit cycle can be understood as a limit cycle that is stable for trajectories on the interior of the limit cycle, and unstable for trajectories on the exterior (or vice versa).
